```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(formex)

## --- tiny inline-SVG helpers, shared by the decision-tree diagrams ----------
## Colours use `currentColor` so the diagrams read in both the light and dark
## site themes; one accent marks the path that was taken.
.accent <- "#2c7fb8"; .unit <- "#2ca25f"

.box <- function(cx, cy, label, chosen = FALSE, muted = FALSE,
                 w = 122, h = 34, accent = .accent) {
  x <- cx - w / 2; y <- cy - h / 2
  if (chosen)
    sprintf(paste0('<rect x="%g" y="%g" rx="7" width="%g" height="%g" fill="%s" ',
      'fill-opacity="0.15" stroke="%s" stroke-width="2"/><text x="%g" y="%g" ',
      'text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" ',
      'font-weight="600" fill="currentColor">%s</text>'),
      x, y, w, h, accent, accent, cx, cy + 4, label)
  else
    sprintf(paste0('<rect x="%g" y="%g" rx="7" width="%g" height="%g" fill="none" ',
      'stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.4" stroke-width="1"%s/><text x="%g" ',
      'y="%g" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" ',
      'fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="%s">%s</text>'),
      x, y, w, h, if (muted) ' stroke-dasharray="4 3"' else "",
      cx, cy + 4, if (muted) "0.4" else "0.55", label)
}
.edge <- function(x1, y1, x2, y2, chosen = FALSE, accent = .accent) {
  if (chosen)
    sprintf('<line x1="%g" y1="%g" x2="%g" y2="%g" stroke="%s" stroke-width="2"/>',
            x1, y1, x2, y2, accent)
  else
    sprintf(paste0('<line x1="%g" y1="%g" x2="%g" y2="%g" stroke="currentColor" ',
            'stroke-opacity="0.22" stroke-width="1"/>'), x1, y1, x2, y2)
}
.glab <- function(t, y)
  sprintf(paste0('<text x="84" y="%g" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" ',
    'font-family="sans-serif" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.5">%s</text>'),
    y + 4, t)
.svg <- function(body, w = 580, h = 400)
  cat(sprintf(paste0('<svg viewBox="0 0 %g %g" role="img" ',
    'style="max-width:100%%;height:auto;margin:1.2em 0" ',
    'xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">%s</svg>'), w, h, paste(body, collapse = "")))
```

When you open an unfamiliar data file, the first thing you need to know about
each column is: **what is this?** Are these dates? dollar amounts? county codes?
people's names? `guess_data_type()` answers that question. You hand it a column
of values and it hands back a `$route` --- its best read of what the column is,
expressed as a path through the package's type **ontology**.

```{r first}
guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"))$route[
  c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_style",
    "depth", "confidence")]
```

The rest of this guide shows how to read that answer, why it is shaped as a
decision tree, and --- most importantly --- why it is allowed to stop early.

## Typing is a walk down a decision tree

The answer is a **path**, four levels deep, from coarse to fine. Typing a column
means starting at the top with a value and walking down, answering one narrowing
question at each step. Here is the full walk for a column of dates like
`03/15/2019`:

```{r tree-date, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.svg(c(
  .glab("value", 38), .glab("data type", 110), .glab("family", 182),
  .glab("type", 254), .glab("format", 326),
  ## faint edges first, chosen edges drawn on top
  .edge(360, 55, 305, 93),  .edge(360, 55, 455, 93),
  .edge(150, 127, 305, 165), .edge(150, 127, 455, 165),
  .edge(150, 199, 305, 237),
  .edge(150, 271, 305, 309), .edge(150, 271, 455, 309),
  .edge(360, 55, 150, 93, TRUE), .edge(150, 127, 150, 165, TRUE),
  .edge(150, 199, 150, 237, TRUE), .edge(150, 271, 150, 309, TRUE),
  ## nodes
  .box(360, 38, "03/15/2019", chosen = TRUE),
  .box(150, 110, "temporal", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 110, "number"),
  .box(455, 110, "text"),
  .box(150, 182, "date", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 182, "time"),
  .box(455, 182, "period"),
  .box(150, 254, "calendar", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 254, "timestamp"),
  .box(150, 326, "mdy_slash", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 326, "ymd_dash"),
  .box(455, 326, "mon_mdy"),
  ## legend
  .edge(20, 372, 44, 372, TRUE),
  '<text x="50" y="376" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.7">path taken</text>',
  .edge(170, 372, 194, 372),
  '<text x="200" y="376" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.7">roads not taken</text>'
))
```

Read it left to right, top to bottom:

1. **`data_type`** --- *how should these be treated?* Not words, not categories,
   not quantities, but points in time. → **`temporal`**.
2. **`semantic_family`** --- *what broad kind of time?* Not a clock time, not a
   span. → **`date`**.
3. **`semantic_type`** --- *what exactly does it mean?* A plain calendar date, not
   a timestamp with a clock attached. → **`calendar`**.
4. **`format_style`** --- *how is it written?* Month first, with slashes. →
   **`mdy_slash`**.

The branches not taken (`number`, `time`, `timestamp`, `ymd_dash` …) are real
alternatives the engine weighed and ruled out. The value column always confirms
it:

```{r route-date}
guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020"))$route[
  c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_style", "depth")]
```

## The bottom of the tree has two facets: *how it's written* and *what it's in*

The leaf level is really two questions, because they are genuinely different.
Take a column of dollar amounts:

```{r tree-usd, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.svg(c(
  .glab("value", 38), .glab("data type", 110), .glab("family", 182),
  .glab("type", 254), .glab("leaf", 326),
  .edge(360, 55, 305, 93),  .edge(360, 55, 455, 93),
  .edge(150, 127, 305, 165), .edge(150, 127, 455, 165),
  .edge(150, 199, 305, 237), .edge(150, 199, 455, 237),
  .edge(360, 55, 150, 93, TRUE), .edge(150, 127, 150, 165, TRUE),
  .edge(150, 199, 150, 237, TRUE),
  .edge(150, 271, 120, 309, TRUE), .edge(150, 271, 360, 309, TRUE, accent = .unit),
  .box(360, 38, "$2,300.00", chosen = TRUE),
  .box(150, 110, "number", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 110, "text"),
  .box(455, 110, "temporal"),
  .box(150, 182, "currency", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 182, "quantity"),
  .box(455, 182, "portion"),
  .box(150, 254, "usd", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 254, "euro"),
  .box(455, 254, "balance"),
  .box(120, 326, "format: usd", chosen = TRUE),
  .box(360, 326, "unit: USD", chosen = TRUE, accent = .unit),
  .edge(20, 372, 44, 372, TRUE),
  '<text x="50" y="376" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.7">format_style &mdash; how it is written</text>',
  .edge(300, 372, 324, 372, TRUE, accent = .unit),
  '<text x="330" y="376" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.7">unit_type &mdash; what it measures</text>'
), h = 400)
```

- **`format_style`** is *how the value is written*. The same amount could arrive
  as `$2,300.00`, `2300`, or `17,298$`. Style controls how you read it in and
  write it back out.
- **`unit_type`** is *what the value is measured in*. `2300` could be dollars or
  euros; a temperature could be °C or °F; `2019` could be a calendar year or a
  *fiscal* year. The unit does not change how the value is written, but it
  changes what it means --- and whether a conversion is even possible.

```{r route-usd}
guess_data_type(c("$2,300.00", "17,298$", "$-45"))$route[
  c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_style")]
```

Reaching *either* facet counts as getting to the bottom. A plain date has a
writing style but no meaningful unit; a bare temperature reading has a unit that
matters more than its style.

## Graceful failure: get the type right first, then go as deep as you can

Real data is messy, and often the values simply do not say enough to reach a
leaf. **This is the single most important thing to understand about
`guess_data_type()`: it stops at the deepest level it can actually defend, and
refuses to force a guess.**

Consider a column of bare whole numbers --- `0, 1, 42, 17`:

```{r tree-stop, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.svg(c(
  .glab("value", 38), .glab("data type", 110), .glab("family", 182),
  .glab("type", 254), .glab("format", 326),
  .edge(360, 55, 305, 93),  .edge(360, 55, 455, 93),
  .edge(150, 127, 305, 165), .edge(150, 127, 455, 165),
  .edge(150, 199, 305, 237), .edge(150, 199, 455, 237),
  .edge(360, 55, 150, 93, TRUE), .edge(150, 127, 150, 165, TRUE),
  .edge(150, 199, 150, 237, TRUE),
  .edge(150, 271, 150, 309),
  .box(360, 38, "0, 1, 42, 17", chosen = TRUE),
  .box(150, 110, "number", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 110, "text"),
  .box(455, 110, "categorical"),
  .box(150, 182, "quantity", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 182, "currency"),
  .box(455, 182, "portion"),
  .box(150, 254, "count", chosen = TRUE), .box(305, 254, "ratio"),
  .box(455, 254, "rate"),
  .box(230, 326, "no distinct written form", muted = TRUE, w = 210),
  '<text x="420" y="322" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.7">&#8592; stops here</text>',
  '<text x="420" y="338" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.55">depth = 3</text>'
), h = 360)
```

```{r route-stop}
guess_data_type(c("0", "1", "42", "17", "3"))$route[
  c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_style", "depth")]
```

The engine is certain these are a **`number`**, and narrows confidently to a
**`count`** --- but a bare integer has no distinctive *written form*, so it stops
at depth 3 rather than invent a leaf. A column whose values are even less
decisive stops sooner still:

```{r route-depth1}
# plain decimals: clearly numeric, but nothing says what kind
guess_data_type(c("3.7", "8.1", "2.9", "5.4"))$route[
  c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "depth")]
```

The `depth` field is exactly how far the walk got:

```
0  unknown        2  the family       4  the leaf (format_style and/or unit_type)
1  the data_type  3  the specific type
```

Why is this the right behavior? Because the **two levels do different jobs**, and
they fail differently:

- **`data_type` is the load-bearing answer.** It decides how a column is
  *profiled* and *treated*: a `number` you can sum and average; an `identifier`
  you must leave alone; a `temporal` you can put on a timeline. Getting this
  level right is the primary measure of success, and it is almost always
  reachable.
- **The leaf is the bonus.** Reaching it unlocks the *exact* recipe for cleaning
  and safely storing the column (see *Formatting Syntax*). It is the goal, but
  missing it only means falling back to the safe, general rule for the level you
  did reach --- never corruption.

So the worst case is never a confidently wrong answer; it is an honest "this far
and no further," left for a column name or a data dictionary to settle. A column
name, when you pass one, is used only as a tie-breaker between leaves the values
already support --- it never overrides the evidence in the values.

## The type:family:type triplet, at a glance

Across a handful of columns, here is what `guess_data_type()` returns --- the
`data_type : semantic_family : semantic_type` triplet, the leaf format, and how
far down each one reached:

```{r triplet-table, echo = FALSE}
examples <- list(
  "03/15/2019, 12/31/2020"   = c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"),
  "2019-03-15, 2020-12-31"   = c("2019-03-15", "2020-12-31"),
  "$2,300.00, 17,298$, $-45" = c("$2,300.00", "17,298$", "$-45"),
  "California, TX, Ohio"      = c("California", "TX", "Ohio", "CA"),
  "06037, 36061, 48201"      = c("06037", "36061", "48201", "17031"),
  "0, 1, 42, 17"             = c("0", "1", "42", "17", "3"),
  "3.7, 8.1, 2.9"            = c("3.7", "8.1", "2.9", "5.4")
)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(examples), function(nm) {
  r <- guess_data_type(examples[[nm]])$route
  data.frame(
    example = nm,
    `data_type : family : type` =
      paste(r$data_type, r$semantic_family, r$semantic_type, sep = " : "),
    format_style = ifelse(is.na(r$format_style), "—", r$format_style),
    depth = r$depth,
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

The clean, unambiguous columns reach depth 4 and name a leaf; the bare numbers
stop short but still get their `data_type` right. That is graceful failure
working exactly as designed.

  the leaf's recipe to clean and standardize the values. That is the second half
